title: Sample ratio mismatch
reading_md:
**What it is.** A sample ratio mismatch (SRM) means the observed split of users differs from the designed split by more than chance allows. It signals a bug in assignment, redirects, logging or filtering. Do not trust the result until the cause is found. The check is a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, and Microsoft uses p < 0.001 as the threshold.

**How to work it out.**

χ² = Σ (observed - expected)² / expected, with degrees of freedom = number of variants - 1

For two variants (1 degree of freedom), the critical value for p = 0.001 is 10.83.

Worked example. A 50/50 design with 10,000 users in control and 9,500 in treatment.

- Total 19,500, so 9,750 expected in each group
- Each group adds 250² / 9,750 = 6.410
- χ² = 12.82 (2 decimals)
- 12.82 > 10.83, so p < 0.001: an SRM

Typical causes are assignment bugs, redirects that lose users in one variant, bot filtering, logging failures and analysis filters that depend on the variant.

**In the interview.** "Treatment has 3% fewer users than control in a 50/50 test. Does it matter?" A good answer: yes, if the chi-square test flags it. Whatever removed those users may be related to the outcome.

**Common mistakes.**

- "Small differences in group size are always fine." With very large samples, even a 50.2% share can be an SRM: in a 2017 talk, Ron Kohavi showed 821,588 against 815,482 users, with p = 1.8e-6.
- Fixing an SRM by reweighting the groups. The users who went missing may differ from the rest, so find the cause.
- Checking the split on converted users only. Check it on all assigned users.
